text:
Recent work supports modeling elapsed time alongside sequence order. [TemProxRec (2024)](https://arxiv.org/abs/2402.09784) distinguishes within-user time gaps from cross-user temporal proximity; [TALE (2024 preprint)](https://arxiv.org/abs/2412.07382) uses interval-dependent item correlations and trend normalization. These motivate temporal features, but their architectures and reported gains do not establish benefits for NextItNet. [NextItNet](https://arxiv.org/abs/1808.05163) supplies the appropriate backbone: residual dilated causal convolutions capturing dependencies across multiple sequence scales.

For complement/substitute intent, [KGSCL (2025)](https://www.sciencedirect.com/science/article/pii/S089360802500070X) uses explicit Amazon metadata relationships to guide substitution and insertion augmentations. Those relationship labels are unavailable here, so its supervision cannot be reproduced. Title similarity, directional purchase transitions and short time gaps provide possible compatibility signals, but none establishes complementarity or substitution. Treat these relationships as latent hypotheses rather than diagnostic ground truth.

A feasible experiment, inferred from these directions: jointly train random-initialized title/description token embeddings, mean pooling and an item-ID projection inside one NextItNet network. Add bucketed log time-gap embeddings or gap-conditioned gates within its causal residual blocks. Use only gaps between observed history events; the next purchase timestamp is unavailable at prediction. Ablate text and time features against the corrected baseline, selecting by macro validation HR@10. This requires neither pretrained weights nor independently fitted scoring components; preserve final-nonpadding readout and matching checkpoint/predictor architecture.
